subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis with too many criteria [Pitfall]
passage: Dilnaz's spreadsheet had thirteen criteria on Monday night. On Tuesday she added the fourteenth, "quality of office chairs", and reweighted everything. On Wednesday she changed learning from 20 percent to 18 and pay from 12 to 14. Her flatmate Darshan looked over her shoulder at midnight. "The deadline is Friday at five." "I know, I know, one more pass." On Thursday she dropped chairs and added "friendly seniors". On Friday afternoon she was still deciding which weighting felt fair. At five past five, an email arrived: the offer she had leaned toward had lapsed, since no reply was received. She stared at the sheet, its cells all neatly coloured, and then at the one offer left.

qa.q: Which criterion did Dilnaz add as the fourteenth?
qa.a: She added 'quality of office chairs' as the fourteenth.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz feeling as she stares at the sheet after the email?
qa.a: She is stunned and regretful: the offer she had leaned toward has lapsed while she kept tinkering.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Dilnaz have used, and why?
qa.a: She could have fixed five criteria and a decision time in advance, because a limit on the process keeps the deadline from disappearing.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Dilnaz's nightly reweighting?
qa.a: Darshan sees the deadline approaching while she keeps adjusting, and reminds her at midnight that it is Friday at five, though she asks for one more pass.

grounding: Shows analysis paralysis: extra criteria and nightly reweighting until the acceptance deadline passes and one offer is lost.
